newsitem.title: CHINA: China assures protection for Taiwan investment.
newsitem.headline: China assures protection for Taiwan investment.

text.p: Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen has promised full protection for Taiwanese business in China and urged arch-rival Taipei not to prevent its entrepreneurs from investing in the mainland.

Political differences should not be allowed to interrupt business exchanges, the foreign minister and vice premier said on Monday before the opening of China's first fair for exports from the southern port city of Xiamen to Taiwan.
"We will not affect or interrupt cross-straits economic cooperation with political differences," the People's Daily on Tuesday quoted Qian as saying.
"Rather we will promote such relationships by encouraging Taiwan business people's investment and follow the law in protecting Taiwan compatriots' investment and expanding trade," he said.
"We will protect their just and reasonable rights and interests," Qian said.
He voiced the hope that the Taiwan authorities would no longer prevent entrepreneurs from investing in the mainland, saying this was not in the interests of Taiwanese business.
Taiwan has banned direct investment in China since a civil war split the two in 1949.
But some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured an estimated US$30 billion through overseas affiliates to fund their investments on the mainland, some without government authorisation.

The Nationalist island has decided to put a cap on local investments in China after footwear giant Pou Chen reportedly invested in setting up a bank in China, and petrochemcial giant Formosa Plastic group reportedly started a thermal power plant project on the mainland.

Although Taiwan has allowed its businessmen to invest indirectly to the mainland since the late 1980s, it still bars them from investing in key industries such as power and auto plants, as well as financial services.

Qian urged the Taiwan authorities to take steps to reduce restrictions on mainland Chinese exports to Taiwan, and to gradually decrease the trade deficit with Taiwan, stressing the need for direct shipping links across the Taiwan Strait.
"We have been unremitting in our efforts to this end," he said.
However, there were signs the first commercial sailings across the Taiwan Strait for nearly five decades could be imminent.

Taiwan transport Vice Minister Mao Chi-kuo said last week direct sailings could take place within 10 days, now that Beijing has approved five mainland shipping firms to pioneer services between the mainland and its island arch-rival.

All must receive formal approval from Taiwan, but Taiwan's transportation ministry said it expected to receive applications from the newly authorised Chinese firms within a few days and would approve them swiftly.
Taipei allows indirect links through Hong Kong or elsewhere but has come under increasing pressure to permit direct shipping and air links from both its own businessmen and from Beijing.
